content.text: I want you to take a look at resurf.so, all its features, and its ui, and the few references photos of it that I think put in the inkling file and screens page in paper. I really want to take inspiration from this app to redesign inkling to it and then simply tweak it slightly so that its follows our vibe and uses our mascot in some way
I'll start by gathering the references: the Paper file, resurf.so itself, and inkling's current UI.

input.prompt: Describe in detail every feature of this product, its UI, layout, visual style (colors, typography, card treatments, navigation, search), and any taglines. Be exhaustive.

result.output:
**Resurf** is a Mac knowledge base and bookmark manager. Its main tagline is **"A Personal Context Library."** The page also describes it as saving notes, bookmarks, screenshots, and PDFs in one local library, then passing that context to AI.

**Note on visual style:** The page text doesn't specify colors, font families, or exact card styling. Those details would only be visible in the screenshots, which I can't see here.

**Navigation and layout**
- Top bar: Story, Roadmap, Updates, Pricing, and a Resources menu (How-to guides, FAQ, Compare apps, Blog, Manage license, Get support), plus a Download button.
- Hero: "Download for Free" and "Buy a license · $39" buttons, with platform links for Mac, iPhone & iPad, the Chrome extension, and MCP/CLI for AI.
- A product carousel with a looping video poster and captioned thumbnails.
- The page uses a split layout with an inspector panel on the right for image details.

**Core features**
- **Quick Capture:** Save notes, links, and screenshots through a global Mac shortcut (⌘⇧C).
- **Inbox:** "Save now, sort later." Items can be assigned, kept for later, or deleted with one key.
- **Library:** A visual view of bookmarks, images, and screenshots together. Selecting an image surfaces similar references.
- **Image details:** Keeps color information. Optional AI generates keywords and a summary.
- **Reader:** A distraction-free view for saved articles.
- **Notes:** A rich-text editor with headings, lists, code, and highlights, saved as Markdown.
- **Spaces and tags:** Group items by project, topic, or idea. Tags appear as hashtags.
- **Search:** Finds items by keywords or by meaning. It runs locally and includes full text of notes, articles, PDFs, and words inside screenshots. The search bar appears to use a ⌘K shortcut and a time filter such as "last 6mo."
- **PDFs:** Open, read, and annotate PDFs inside the app, with notes beside the source.
- **Highlighting and annotation:** Available for articles and PDFs.
- **Voice memos:** Record thoughts directly into the library.
- **AI summaries (opt-in):** Short summaries and read-time estimates for articles, links, and PDFs.
- **Bring Your Own AI (opt-in):** Use your own API key, such as OpenAI, or connect agents through MCP or the CLI on Mac.
- **Ask Your Library (opt-in):** Ask questions across saved content.

**Supported formats:** Articles, PDFs, images, audio, video, YouTube, tweets, GitHub, code, and notes.

**Storage and sync**
- Stored locally in a Resurf folder under the user's Library directory.
- Works offline.
- Optional private iCloud sync. No Resurf account is required.

**Platforms**
- **Mac:** Requires macOS 14.3 or later, on Apple Silicon or Intel. Free to try.
- **iPhone and iPad:** Free. Save links from the share sheet and browse the library.
- **Chrome extension:** Available separately.
- Built as a native Swift app.

**Pricing:** Free to try, with a paid license listed at $39.

content.text:
I've designed four screens on a new **"resurf redesign"** page in the inkling Paper file. The *screens* page is untouched. These are mockups only; I haven't changed any code.

**The screens**
- **A · Library:** Resurf's three-pane layout in our dark palette.
  - The sidebar keeps our real nav (Everything, Top of mind, Serendipity, Spaces), with counts lined up on the right.
  - Each Space gets an ink-blot icon in its own colour: the mascot's body without the eyes.
  - The grid sits in a rounded panel under a centered "Everything 1,601" title. Tiles have no card chrome and still look different by type (quote, article, note, video, PDF).
  - The search bar is gone. There's a search icon next to Add, and a small grid/list switch floats at the bottom.
- **B · Search drops in:** the bar slides down from the top edge over a fade. The mascot is the search icon inside the bar.
- **C · Query pinned:** once you've searched, the bar goes away and the query stays as a chip with "Add filter", a result count and Clear. A filtered grid always shows what it's filtered by.
- **D · Item open:** the image on a dotted background with a zoom control, plus a Resurf-style side panel. It has Info and Similar tabs, colour swatches, your title and note, Space chips, manual tags, details, and star/folder/trash actions.

**What I took out of Resurf on purpose**
- Their "Beta" badges, sparkle AI buttons, AI-written summaries and tags, and the "6 by meaning" count. All of these show AI to the user, which our rules don't allow.
- Inbox, Starred and Tags as nav items, because inkling doesn't have them. An Inbox for triage is the one Resurf feature worth a real discussion later, but it's a feature, not a restyle.

**Things to know**
- I only found one Resurf screenshot in Paper, on the *references* page. If you meant to add more to *screens*, they didn't save. I got the rest from resurf.so's product tour in the preview browser.
- On your hidden-search idea: as above, I'd open it by typing, `/`, `Ctrl+K` or clicking the icon, and skip the gesture.

**Open questions before any code**
1. Is the dark palette right, or do you want to try Resurf's light look as a second option?
2. Should the open item use the side panel (screen D) instead of our current full overlay? That's the biggest structural change here.
3. Do you want a Similar-tab screen, and a list view to go with the grid/list switch?

5. At the end, take final screenshots at scale 1 and compare them to the backups pixel-for-pixel by eye, region by region (sidebar, toolbar, grid, overlays). Call `finish_working_on_nodes`.

- Remove redundant wrapper frames that add nothing (a single-child frame with no styles that affect layout or paint). Only if removing it provably changes nothing.
- Replace leftover `position: absolute` + hardcoded left/top inside flex layouts with equivalent flex layout ONLY when the result is identical. Absolute positioning that is genuinely needed (overlays, scrims, floating bars, fades) stays.

- Do not change any visible colour, size, spacing, font, text content, radius, image, or z-order.
- Do not delete nodes with opacity 0 or that look invisible; they may represent animation states.
- Do not use the `background` shorthand in update_styles (it has been seen to wipe layout properties); use backgroundColor / backgroundImage individually. Paper does not support `margin`; use padding/gap/spacers.
- `position:absolute` inside a `write_html` subtree can be silently dropped, so prefer `update_styles`, `move_nodes`, `rename_nodes`, `delete_nodes` over rewriting HTML.
- Do not touch any artboard outside your scope.

Reply with a short list per artboard: what you changed, anything you deliberately left alone and why, and whether the final screenshot matched the backup exactly. Be honest about any difference.

I'm in, as long as it's an accent on one or two surfaces and not the whole interface.

**Why I'd hold back on the library itself:**
- **GPU cost:** it renders live glass with WebGPU, redrawing whatever sits behind the glass. In inkling that's the card grid, which moves every time the user scrolls, so the GPU would be busy constantly. AGENTS.md specifically rules out effects that keep repainting, because they peg the GPU on high-refresh displays.

**What I'd do instead:** build the glass ourselves with CSS and SVG filters, using `backdrop-filter` with a little edge distortion and a bright rim. That gets most of the look. content.text:
I read all eight. Most of them confirm my earlier take, but four are interesting for different reasons.

## Ruled out
- **electron-liquid-glass:** it's macOS 26 only, and on Windows its calls do nothing. Some of its features use private Apple APIs the author labels "DO NOT USE IN PROD".
- **LiquidGlassReference:** it's not a library. It's one README about Apple's iOS 26 Liquid Glass in SwiftUI, which the author wrote so Claude has the docs when building glass. There's nothing in it for the web.
- **fluidglass:** it runs a fluid simulation (Navier-Stokes plus reaction-diffusion). That's a demo that animates all the time, the exact thing AGENTS.md bans. It also has no license.
- **liquid-dom:** this one surprised me. It copies the live page into the GPU using Chrome's experimental HTML-in-Canvas API, which is behind `chrome://flags`. It's the technically "correct" way to refract live content, so it's worth watching, but no user has that flag on. It also needs React 19 and WebGPU.

## Interesting
- **liquidGL:** it bends a snapshot of the page, not the live page. Scrolling works through sync hooks, but you have to register anything that changes (`registerDynamic()`), and CSS animations don't refresh the snapshot. Images also need permissive CORS headers. Our card grid has lazy loading, hover effects and new cards arriving from capture, so it would show stale content. The useful part: its last fallback is plain `backdrop-filter`, so even the authors treat CSS as the safety net.
- **plasma-ui:** it has the best idea in the batch. One shared WebGL canvas draws every panel, and panels touching each other merge like liquid. It has a `freezeOnScroll` option and caps panels at 16. Still, the README says it's GPU-heavy, every pass covers the full viewport, it's pre-1.0, and it doesn't run well on mobile. That's too heavy for an app that's mostly a scrolling grid.
- **liquid-glass-studio:** a playground, not a package. It's a good reference for tuning: superellipse shapes, dispersion (colour fringing at the edges), Fresnel glare, and "blob" merging. I'd use the online demo to pick our values.
- **archisvaze/liquid-glass:** ⭐ this is the approach I suggested. An SVG `feDisplacementMap` inside `backdrop-filter`, with the displacement map computed from a real refractive index, so the edge distortion is physically plausible rather than a random wobble. It's MIT licensed, plain HTML/JS, and works only in Chromium, which is all Electron needs. It also has a WebGL version.

## What I'd do now
Build our own small `<Glass>` component, using **archisvaze's displacement math** with **values tuned in liquid-glass-studio**. It costs nothing when nothing moves, needs no canvas or snapshot, and adds no dependency. Keep plasma-ui's merging panels as an idea for later, for example the search bar and filter chips merging together.

Want me to build the HTML prototype now? It would put the search bar and zoom pill over a scrolling card grid, with sliders for refractive index, blur and rim.

59:The liquid-glass renderer requires WebGPU. DOM-backed `Html` content also requires the experimental HTML-in-Canvas API, which is currently available only behind Chrome's Canvas Draw Element flag: `chrome://flags/#canvas-draw-element`. The implementation uses `<canvas layoutsubtree>` and canvas paint events to copy live DOM content into GPU textures.
61:The DOM and React packages can build scene graphs in any browser-like environment, but rendering requires a browser with `navigator.gpu`; rendering DOM-backed content additionally requires the Chrome flag above. Three integrations require Three's WebGPU renderer, not WebGLRenderer.

content.text:
I'm done testing. liquid-dom runs in our version of Electron, and here's how it compares with plain CSS glass.

**liquid-dom**, with real refraction over the live, scrolling grid:
![liquid-dom glass over a scrolling inkling grid](C:\Users\chris\AppData\Local\Temp\agents\chat-images\resurf-redesign\ink-glass-mid.jpg)

**Plain CSS glass** (`backdrop-filter`), same page:
![CSS backdrop-filter glass over the same grid](C:\Users\chris\AppData\Local\Temp\agents\chat-images\resurf-redesign\ink-css-mid.jpg)

## What I found
- **It works in our Electron with one line.** Electron 44 runs Chromium 152, and the experimental API is available once we add `app.commandLine.appendSwitch('enable-blink-features', 'CanvasDrawElement')`. Users never touch a flag, because we ship the browser. That removes my main objection from before.
- **The look is clearly better.** The search bar bends the cards at its edges like real glass. CSS can only blur.
- **Performance, scrolling for 4 seconds on this 75Hz display:**

  | | Average frame | Hitches (>25ms) | Worst frame | JS cost per frame |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | CSS glass | 13.3ms | 0 | 13.7ms | ~0ms |
  | liquid-dom | 14.3ms | 5 | **120ms** | 1.6ms |

  The hitches are visible stutters, most likely when new card images scroll in and have to be uploaded to the GPU. That's the kind of dropped frame AGENTS.md says users should never notice.
- **It redraws every frame by default.** Its demos run a loop that never stops, which breaks our rule against animations that keep repainting. We'd have to redraw only while scrolling or while something is moving. That should be doable, but it's our code to write and test.
- **Risk:** it depends on an experimental Chrome API that could change or be removed in a future Electron upgrade. Electron also logged a GPU error when the window closed. The fallback would be the CSS version, so the app wouldn't break, it would just lose the effect.

**About fluidglass:** I agree it looks the most real. That comes from its glass shader, the refraction and light at the edges. The fluid simulation underneath is what makes it run constantly. Its shader is the part we'd borrow, not its engine.

**What I'd suggest:** liquid-dom for the search bar and zoom pill, with redrawing only while scrolling, as an experiment we can switch off and fall back to CSS. First I'd want to get those stutters down, for example by redrawing only on change and keeping images uploaded to the GPU between frames, then measure again. Want me to try that? Everything is in a scratch folder outside the repo (`%TEMP%\glassproto`), so nothing in inkling has changed.

content.text:
Both problems are fixed in the prototype, and liquid-dom now scrolls as smoothly as the plain CSS version.

![liquid-dom glass with thumbnails, redrawn only on change](C:\Users\chris\AppData\Local\Temp\agents\chat-images\resurf-redesign\ink-glass-demand-thumb-mid.jpg)

Each run scrolls for 4 seconds on this 75Hz display:

| Setup | Average frame | Hitches (>25ms) | Worst frame | Glass redraws while idle |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| liquid-dom as it ships | 14.4ms | 5 | 133ms | **75/sec** |
| + redraw only on change | 14.3ms | 5 | 120ms | ~0 |
| + images decoded in advance | 14.5ms | 5 | 133ms | 0 |
| + **thumbnails** | **13.3ms** | **0** | **13.6ms** | ~0 |
| plain CSS glass | 13.3ms | 0 | 14.4ms | 0 |

**What fixed what:**
1. **Constant redrawing:** I only redraw the glass after a scroll or after the page repaints. With nothing moving it does nothing, which meets the AGENTS.md rule. It's about 10 lines around the library and needs no changes inside it.
2. **The stutters:** the demo images were the originals at up to 6000×4000. The copy of the page behind the glass had to redraw each one as it scrolled in. Shrunk to 560px wide, the stutters are gone. Decoding them in advance didn't help; their size was the problem. The real grid already uses thumbnails, so this matches how inkling works.

**Caveats:**
- I tested one machine with an automated, perfectly smooth scroll. I haven't tried a weak laptop GPU, a 144Hz display, or real wheel and trackpad scrolling.
- The app's card grid is virtualized, and I haven't tested a virtualized grid inside liquid-dom's copy of the page.
- The experimental-API risk is unchanged. We'd need the CSS version as an automatic fallback.

**My recommendation:** it's good enough to be worth trying in the real app as an experiment. Start with only the search bar and zoom pill, behind a check that falls back to CSS glass. If you want, I'll add a short note to this redesign's plan, or move on to mocking the glass look into the Paper frames. Everything is still in `%TEMP%\glassproto`, and nothing in the repo has changed.

Use: liquid-dom (WebGPU). Electron 44 = Chromium 152, which has the HTML-in-Canvas API behind enable-blink-features=CanvasDrawElement. We ship the browser, so users never see a flag.
Only on floating chrome over the grid: search bar, zoom pill. Panels and sidebar stay solid.
Render on demand: redraw on scroll and canvas paint events only. Never the demo's rAF loop (75 redraws/s idle → ~0).
Thumbnails only under glass. Full-size 6000px JPEGs caused 120ms hitches; 560px thumbs: 0 hitches, matches CSS (13.3ms frames at 75Hz).
Fallback: CSS backdrop-filter blur + rim when WebGPU or the API is missing. The API is experimental and could go away in an Electron upgrade.
Look: fluidglass's glass shader (edge light, refraction) is the target feel. Not its fluid sim, which runs nonstop.
Untested: weak laptop GPUs, 144Hz, real wheel/trackpad scroll, the virtualized grid.

I'd turn the centered **"Everything"** title into the search field itself. It would be one wide glass bar in the middle of the toolbar that reads like a title until you click it.

- **Shape:** about 380–420px wide and 34px tall, the same height as the pills, so the toolbar reads as one clean row.
- **Material:** the dark glass we just settled on. It's the biggest glass surface over the grid, so it's where the effect shows best.

how would you suggest we start putting the screens into the app. like what order or what would be the most efficient way too

I'd go from shared pieces out to individual screens, one PR per step so each is easy to review.

1. **Glass as a shared style.** Make one CSS class or token set from the dark glass recipe and use plain CSS `backdrop-filter`. Everything after this uses it, so it goes first. The WebGPU liquid-dom version can come much later as its own experiment. It's riskier and behind an experimental Chromium flag.

2. **App shell: toolbar and edge tab.** Do the toolbar layout first: back/forward pill on the left, title in the middle, Add on the right. Then build the edge tab with its flip animation in place of the round sidebar toggle. Every screen sits inside this shell, so getting it right once fixes it everywhere.

3. **Search pill, then the morph into the search bar.** This is the most visible change, and the search bar with the mascot eyes is already built. Do it in two steps: first the resting pill that opens the existing bar, then the grow animation. That way, if the morph needs tuning, it doesn't hold up the layout.

4. **Item view.**
   - Glass title pill and history pill.
   - Close/esc in place of "×", and no more "⋯".
   - The new action bar: open original, show in folder, archive.
   - The "Belongs to" row.

   It's mostly reshuffling controls that already exist, so it should be quick once steps 1 and 2 are in.

5. **Settings.** It mostly inherits the shell and glass, so it's a small pass to restyle it to match 3.1 and 3.2.

6. **Pixel zoom.** It's self-contained and nothing depends on it, so it goes last.

Detail views for the other item types (article, PDF, note) aren't designed yet. We'd mock those up before step 4 touches them, or step 4 ships for images only.

To keep it moving, I'd do each step on its own branch, check it in preview (`bun run dev`) with the demo library, and you look at a screenshot before it becomes a PR. Steps 1–3 depend on each other, so they go in order. Steps 4–6 could run in parallel worktrees once the shell lands.

The Forward fix is pushed as `bc69b04`. The Find similar case itself has only been checked by reading the code, not run, because Find similar only works in the desktop app.

**Cause:** going back passed through an in-between state on the way to the step you asked for, and that in-between state was being saved as a brand-new step. Saving a new step clears everything ahead of it, so Forward greyed out. A search typed just before going back could also save an outdated step after the fact.

**Fix:** going back or forward now restores the step without saving anything new, and a late search save is thrown away if you've already moved.

**Checked:** in the web preview, Luna went Back four times and then Forward four times through a view change, a Space, a search and an open item, and every step came back. The lint and typecheck on the changed code passed.

Want me to have Luna re-run the desktop test to confirm the Find similar case? The five design questions from the gap list are still open too.

The three Haiku fix agents hit the session usage limit before making any edits. It has reset now, so I've restarted all three from where they stopped. Each is fixing part of the comparison's list:

1. **Search:** the pinned search query covers the first card, and there's a copper focus ring on the open search bar that Paper doesn't have.
2. **Item view:** the window's minimise, maximise and close buttons sit on top of the item view's close button. That happens in the full app too, so you currently can't click it with the mouse. Paper's 8px spacing around the photo and side panel is also missing.
3. **Sidebar:** the logo is 44px where Paper has 26px, and the bottom padding is 10px where Paper has 6px.

The web preview server stopped when it hit its time limit. I'll start it again once these land, then do one pass in the app myself and show you the screenshots before committing.

**Position math:** the logo's centre was already at Paper's offset from the first nav row, because the header and nav move together under the 39px band. The gap was off only because of the 44px box. With the 26px visual centred at the same point, the logo sits at (16, 44) in the app and "Everything" starts at y=97. Paper's logo is at (16, 23) and "Everything" at y=76, both shifted by the 21px band, so the logo-to-nav gap is 27px in both.

The roaming body is still 44px, though. The mascot will look 26px docked and 44px while it roams, so it grows on the hop out and shrinks on the way back. That needs a decision: a per-anchor size in the roam engine would fix it, but it touches the single-size constraint.

**Open points:**
- Paper's logo is a 37.5-unit viewBox drawn at 26px, and the engine's blot fills about 63% of its box. A 26px box therefore gives about a 16px blot, which may look smaller than Paper's ink. - **Resting ring is effectively unreachable.** `onFocus` sets `isSearchFocused` on the same tick, so keyboard focus expands the bar immediately. Cards scroll directly underneath, so the blur is recomputed continuously. The top bar combines 18px blur with saturation and brightness, and the bottom fade adds two more blur layers. This is the main cost while scrolling.
- **The whole library reloads on a timer.** Every 30 seconds — and again after background-job updates settle (400ms trailing pause) — the app re-fetches every item and every item's job status, rebuilds every card object, and re-renders the visible grid. On a large library that's a lot of repeated work for a handful of changed items.
- **File capture handles the entire file up front.** Picking or dropping a file reads it completely into the UI, expands it into an array of individual numbers, sends that across, then writes it and, for images, builds the thumbnail before the card appears. Large images, PDFs, or videos can freeze capture and use many times the file size in memory.

### While browsing

- **Opening an item animates its position and size.** The overlay and everything inside it — image, inspector, toolbar — recalculates layout on every frame of the open/close flight. Animating a scaled/translated snapshot would be much cheaper.
- **Switching grid/list clones every visible card.** Each clone includes its image, and each clone is measured repeatedly. On a large window this is a visible hitch.
- **Opening or closing the sidebar animates width and padding,** so the whole grid reflows for the full 300ms.
- **Panning a zoomed image re-renders the viewer on every pointer move** instead of just moving the image.
- **Every new search result remounts the entire masonry grid.** That recreates all visible cards and images and resets video/embed state. The reset is intentional, but the cost is paid on every result change.

### Search and data

- **Semantic search reads and compares every stored embedding in one pass,** on the same part of the app that serves files and handles storage. As the library grows, search and the Similar tab get slower and can hold up other work.
- **Every refresh asks for job statuses for every item in one query.** Large libraries create a very large query and can hit the database's limit; only active/failed jobs or changes since the last refresh are needed.
- **The Archive tab loads, converts, and draws every archived item at once,** and requests job summaries for all of them. A few hundred archived items means a lot of cards and images at once.

### Files, media, and settings

- **The local asset handler reads each requested file fully into memory,** with no cache headers and no range support. Large images/PDFs and video seeking can re-read whole files, and repeated grid mounts can do it again.
- **Locally saved video cards load the real video file just to show a frame.** A poster or thumbnail until play would avoid reading the file while scrolling.
- **Opening Settings walks every asset file one at a time** to compute library size, every time. The backend has a cache, but the UI always asks for a fresh scan.

### Background

- **The mascot redraws a detailed SVG through React on every animation frame, in two places, all the time,** even when idle or the sidebar is collapsed. It's intentional, but it's why the app never truly idles. Pausing when not visible, or drawing directly instead of through React, would remove the constant cost.

If you only take three: incremental library refresh, lighter/targeted glass blur over the grid, and a streaming file handoff."

| Finding | Verdict | From main or branch | Impact at ~2,000 items on Windows | Fix and size |

| 30-second and job-event reloads | **PARTLY TRUE** | **Main.** | A refresh fetches all listed items, queries their job summaries, converts every item, and passes a new array to the grid. The grid is virtualized. | Keep the fallback refresh, but reconcile unchanged items by stable identity and update job summaries incrementally. **M** |
| File capture reads and sends the whole file | **TRUE-FIX** | **Main.** | `Array.from(Uint8Array)` expands each byte into a JS number before IPC; a 50 MB file can create substantial memory and copy overhead. Image thumbnail generation is awaited before the item is returned and shown. | Send an `ArrayBuffer`/`Uint8Array` over IPC and make thumbnail work a background job after the item is saved. **M** |
| Opening an item animates its position and size | **PARTLY TRUE** | **Main:** the rectangle flight already existed; this branch changes the overlay presentation. | GSAP animates the dialog’s `left/top/width/height` for one brief flight. That can trigger layout, but the inspector is hidden during the flight, so “everything inside recalculates” overstates it. The cost is limited to opening or closing one item. | — |
| Grid/list switch clones and measures visible cards | **TRUE-INTENTIONAL** | **Main.** | It clones mounted cards, including media, and reads layout several times during the transition. Virtualization limits this to the visible set; cost is transient and only on a view switch. | — |
| Sidebar animation reflows the grid | **TRUE-INTENTIONAL** | **Main.** | The 300 ms width/padding transitions change the main content geometry and cause grid layout work, but only during an occasional sidebar toggle. | — |
| Panning a zoomed image rerenders on pointer move | **PARTLY TRUE** | **Main.** | Each pointer move updates React state, but the state belongs to the image-stage component; it does not rerender the whole overlay. The image transform changes during the drag. | — |
| Search results remount the masonry grid | **TRUE-INTENTIONAL** | **Main.** | A changed result-ID list changes `libraryGridKey`, remounting the virtualized grid and resetting mounted card state. This avoids position-keyed cards showing the wrong item after filtering. Only mounted cards and their media are recreated. | — |
| Semantic search brute-forces embeddings on the main process | **TRUE-INTENTIONAL** | **Main.** | The main process loads matching vectors and scores them in a loop. At 2,000 items this is a few million vector operations, likely modest; it can briefly occupy the process that also handles storage and asset requests. A vector index is not justified at this scale without evidence of a delay. | — |
| Job statuses use one `IN` list of every item ID | **PARTLY TRUE** | **Main.** | The query binds one parameter per item. The local Node SQLite build reports `MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER=32766`, so 2,000 IDs are below that limit; the Electron package’s embedded build was not queried separately. The query is still linear in library size and could exceed a lower-limit build or a much larger library. | Batch IDs if libraries approach the runtime limit. **S**, but not urgent at 2,000. |
| Archive loads and renders all archived items | **TRUE-FIX** | **Main.** | Opening Settings fetches all archived items and summaries, converts them, then renders every archived card in a regular grid. A large archive can make Settings open slowly and create many DOM nodes; this path is not virtualized. | Load when the Archive tab opens and virtualize its cards. **M** |
| Asset handler reads full files; no range or cache headers | **TRUE-FIX** | **Main.** | Each GET reads the entire requested asset into memory and returns no range or cache headers. Thumbnails are usually small, but videos and PDFs can be large; concurrent visible media can increase memory use. | Stream files and support byte ranges; add suitable local asset cache headers. **M** |
| Local video cards load the video file to show a frame | **TRUE-FIX** | **Main.** | Cards render a `<video>` using `item.fileUrl` with `preload="metadata"` and seek to 0.01s. Only visible cards do this, but the current asset handler turns that request into a full-file read. | Generate a small poster in background and use it in the card; load the original in the detail view. **M** |
| Settings recomputes library size on every open | **TRUE-FIX** | **Branch:** the size API/cache and Settings call are new here. | `getLibrarySize()` defaults to `refresh=true`; the backend recursively stats files sequentially, bypassing its cached result. With thousands of assets, Settings opening can wait on thousands of filesystem operations. | Use a short-lived cached value on open and refresh it asynchronously or after library writes. **S/M** |
| Mascot continuously redraws in two places | **TRUE-INTENTIONAL** | **Main.** | The shared mascot loop samples a frame each animation frame and updates subscribed figures, including the sidebar and search mascot. **What I’d fix first:**

1. Remove the file-capture byte-array expansion and stop waiting for image thumbnails before showing the saved item.
2. Add streaming and range support to the local asset handler; it currently magnifies video loading costs.
3. Avoid rebuilding unchanged library items on every periodic or job-event refresh.
4. Virtualize the Archive view and defer loading it until that tab is selected.
5. Stop forcing a sequential asset scan whenever Settings opens; refresh the size in the background or after writes.

I’d leave the glass and one-shot transition costs alone for now; they are deliberate visual choices with bounded impact. The job-status parameter limit is not a practical issue at 2,000 items, though batching is a small future-proofing option.

content.text:
Three of the four agents stopped partway when the usage limit hit. It has reset now and all three are working again from where they stopped:
- video posters (Sonnet);
- capture bytes and background thumbnails (Sonnet);
- the Archive tab (Haiku).

The asset handler agent finished before the limit hit:
- **Streaming:** `electron/asset-response.mjs` now serves files as a stream instead of reading each one fully into memory.
- **Byte ranges:** a request for part of a file gets just that part (206). A range past the end of the file is refused (416). A malformed range gets the whole file.
- **Security:** the existing checks that keep requests inside the assets folder are unchanged.
- **Caching:** files get `ETag` and `Last-Modified` but no `Cache-Control`, because thumbnails are rewritten in place under the same name. These headers may do nothing, since nobody has confirmed Chromium caches custom-scheme responses.
- **Checks:** its 15 tests pass and typecheck is clean. It hasn't been run in the actual app yet.

I also added `stream: true` to the `app` scheme in `electron/main.mjs`. Without it, Chromium can't stream or seek video and audio from that scheme, so the range support wouldn't help playback.

When the other three finish I'll check them together, commit, push, and open the perf PR against `feat/glass-surface`.

content.text:
The Archive tab change is done and I've reviewed it:
- **When it loads:** only while the Archive tab is open, and again each time you open it. It no longer loads with Settings or fetches processing details for every item.
- **Rendering:** only the rows near the scroll position are drawn, so the grid's tile size, spacing and tab order stay the same.
- **Checks:** its 6 tests pass, and Biome and typecheck are clean. It hasn't been looked at in the app yet; I'll do that in the UI pass.

Two side effects are worth knowing about:
- **Tab count:** the number next to "Archive" now only shows after you open that tab, because nothing reads the archive before then. Showing it earlier would need a cheap count query in the backend.
- **Row sizes:** `src/components/ArchiveGrid.tsx` hard-codes the tile and row sizes from `App.css`. If those styles change without it, rows will drift while scrolling. A comment there says so.

I'm still waiting on the video poster and capture agents.

<result>Local video cards now show a background-generated poster in the grid instead of loading the video file.

**Correction to the handoff:** I never edited `electron/thumbnail.mjs`. The `inspectImage` changes there are the image-thumbnail agent's, and I left them alone.

**Files changed**
- `electron/video-poster.mjs` (new)

- `src/App.tsx`
- `src/App.css`

**Generation**
- `saveFile` queues a silent `video_poster` job ahead of the embedding job, so capture never waits on it. Imported videos with no thumbnail get one too.
- The job calls `nativeImage.createThumbnailFromPath` at 512px and stores the result as `thumbnail.webp`. I generalised `storePdfThumbnail` into one shared function; the PDF path still works.
- If the shell returns nothing or throws (including Linux), the job retries 3 times, then fails for good. The item stays and the card keeps the typed artwork.

**Backfill:** `onIdle` enqueues one candidate at a time. It picks only videos with a local file, no thumbnail and no earlier failed poster job.

**Cards**
- With a poster: the image and pill, as before. No `<video>` is loaded in the grid any more.
- Without one: the typed `FileArtwork` ("VIDEO", title) using the `file-card` layout. This also covers embeds with no poster, and preview mode (the sample clip now shows typed artwork).
- Layout: the card is 300px tall without a poster and 190px with one, so it shrinks when the poster arrives.
- The detail `<video>` now has `poster`.
- I removed the dead `.video-art` CSS.

**Tests:** `bun test electron/video-poster.test.ts` gives 6 pass. They cover the poster being written and recorded, three failure modes that stop retrying, and backfill picking only the right videos. `bunx biome check` on the changed files and `bun run typecheck` both exit 0.

**Not verified**
- 12 tests in `ai-jobs.test.ts` and `storage.test.ts` fail. Eleven fail because `saveFile` now rejects `number[]` bytes, which is the capture agent's change, so those tests need `Uint8Array`. One is a Windows path-separator assertion in `storage.test.ts`. A scratch run confirmed the refactored PDF thumbnail path still works.
- Nothing was run in the real app or on a real video.
- I skipped the changelog line because AGENTS.md says to ask first.</result>

- **Eleven** fail because the still-running capture change no longer accepts the old number-array bytes; those tests need updating to match.
- **One** is a Windows path-separator assertion in `storage.test.ts`.

I'll check both once the capture agent finishes, which is the last one still running.

# Changelog

All notable development phases and changes are recorded here. See also [roadmap.md](roadmap.md) for what comes next.

The best times to update this file so as to minimize friction while working with a developer or contributor are:
1. When completing a medium-large implementation pass of features, bug fixes, performance enhancements, refactoring updates, or likewise changes
2. The user indicates, whether directly or indirectly through their actions, they want to or are going to finish up the local work and merge the changes afterwards
3. Before starting a new, unrelated task — close out the entry for the work just finished rather than letting it blur or get jumbled into the next thing

Changelog entry format: 

- Follow [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/): group entries under `Added`, `Changed`, `Fixed`, `Removed`, `Deprecated`, `Security`.
- Each entry is one line, written for a human reader — what changed in simple technical terms that someone could understand with simple google searches, not a commit message or file diff summary.
- Reference issue/PR numbers or ticket IDs when they exist

The thumbnail comes from a queued `image_thumbnail` job on a second worker, so OCR and model loading can't delay it. The existing queue handles leases and recovery after a restart. Until the thumbnail lands, the card shows the original image.

**Video posters.** A `video_poster` job on the same worker makes a poster with Electron's `nativeImage.createThumbnailFromPath`, which uses the shell thumbnailer and adds no dependency. Existing videos get theirs from an idle backfill. Grid cards no longer contain a `<video>` element. A video without a poster shows the typed video card instead of an empty dark tile.

**Assets.** The asset handler moved to `electron/asset-response.mjs`. It streams files and supports single byte-range requests (206 and 416), with `ETag` and `Last-Modified` but no `Cache-Control`, because thumbnails are rewritten in place. The `app` scheme now has the `stream` privilege so media can seek. The path containment checks are unchanged.

**Archive.** The archive is read only while its tab is shown. Its grid mounts only the rows near the scroll position and keeps the CSS grid layout and tab order.

**Tests.** There are focused tests for each part. The one failing test in `storage.test.ts` ("portable precedence", a Windows path separator) already fails on main.

The four performance fixes are done, committed and pushed. They're in draft PR [#174](https://github.com/Squidys-Tools/inkling/pull/174), which is stacked on #170 and linked to this thread. None of it has been run in the real app yet: no screenshots, and no test against a real video file.

**What changed:**
- **Capture:** file bytes go to the backend as binary data instead of a number array, so they're much smaller over IPC. The card appears as soon as the file is saved; the thumbnail is made in the background and picks up again after a restart.
- **Video posters:** a background job makes a poster image for each local video, using Windows' own thumbnailer (no new dependency). Existing videos get one gradually while the app is idle. Cards no longer load the video file, and a video without a poster shows the video artwork instead of the empty dark tile.
- **Assets:** library files are streamed instead of read whole into memory, and requests for part of a file work. Large videos and PDFs should start sooner, and videos can seek.
- **Archive tab:** it reads the archive only when you open the tab, and only draws the cards near the scroll position.
- **Settings size** (pushed to #170): the last measured library size shows straight away and refreshes in the background.

**What I changed in the agents' work:**
- Image cards show the original until the thumbnail is ready, as they did before. The agent had them show a placeholder, which would have stuck forever on any image whose thumbnail fails, and on older images that never had one.
- I put video posters on the same worker as image thumbnails, so neither waits behind OCR.
- I enabled streaming for the app's internal file scheme. Without it, videos couldn't seek even with the range support.

**Checks:** 86 of 87 tests pass across the touched files. The one failure is a Windows path-separator test that, per its agent, already failed on `main`. Typecheck and Biome are clean.

**Side effects you'll notice:**
- A video card is taller until its poster arrives, then shrinks once.
- The number next to "Archive" in Settings only shows after you've opened that tab.

**Next:**
- One run in the real app, with before/after screenshots for #174.
- The two optional items, faster library refresh and batched job-status lookups, haven't been started.

content.text:
I've started GPT-6 Luna (high) on an end-to-end test of the perf branch and the redesign. It will use the desktop app for anything native and the browser preview where that's enough, with a scratch library rather than your real one. It's test-only, so it won't change any code. Screenshots go to `C:\Users\chris\AppData\Local\Temp\agents\chat-images\perf-e2e\`. I'll pass its results on when it finishes.

## The two optional items

### 1. Incremental library refresh (medium)
When the library reloads, for example after you capture something or a background job finishes, the renderer rebuilds everything from scratch (`src/App.tsx:3805–3823`):
1. It asks the backend for the whole list of items.
2. It asks for the processing status of every one of them.
3. It rebuilds every card's data, including working out each one's image URL.
4. It replaces the grid's whole list.

With a few hundred items that's fine. With thousands, every finished OCR or embedding job means an IPC round trip carrying the full list, then rebuilding every card's data. The cards on screen also re-render, even though usually only one item changed.

The fix would be for the backend to report which item ids changed, so the renderer updates just those and leaves the rest alone. It's on the optional list because the cost only shows in large libraries, and it touches the most delicate code in `App.tsx`. That refresh code already re-applies note edits and pins you made in this session so a reload can't overwrite them, and an incremental path has to keep that working.

### 2. Batching the job-status lookup (small)
The processing status comes from `getForItems` in `electron/storage.mjs:811`. It builds one SQL query with one `?` per item, so `item_id IN (?, ?, ?, …)` can end up with thousands of placeholders. Two smaller problems:
- **Size limit:** SQLite caps how many `?` one query can have (32,766 in current builds). A library past that size would make this query fail and break the reload.
- **Wasted work:** it returns every job the item has ever had, finished ones included, and the renderer then discards all but the latest of each kind. That history keeps growing.

The fix would be to run the query in chunks of a few hundred ids, and to ask SQL only for the latest job of each kind per item. It's small and independent of everything else, so it could go into #174 now if you want it.

I'd do #2 now and leave #1 until the library is big enough to feel it, or until after the redesign lands.

input.prompt:
You are making one performance change in inkling, an Electron + React + TypeScript + Vite app with node:sqlite in the main process (Bun 1.4.2). Read AGENTS.md at the worktree root first and follow it. Pay particular attention to "A note on taste": the maintainer wants the smallest model that makes the behavior unsurprising, not clever machinery.

WORKSPACE: C:\Users\chris\.t3\worktrees\inkling\perf-library-io (branch perf/library-io). Work ONLY there.
- Another agent is running a test-only end-to-end pass in this worktree. Do not build, launch Electron or dev servers, or touch .artifacts.
- Use the Edit tool for targeted edits. Do not rewrite src/App.tsx with Write.
- Run NO git commands that change state. The maintainer commits.

PROBLEM: in src/App.tsx, the library load effect (around line 3800, the one using listActiveItems / searchItems, countActiveJobs and getProcessingSummaries) rebuilds the entire library whenever it refreshes. It does so after a capture, and when a background job finishes and the backend announces an item/job update:
1. It fetches every item over IPC.
2. It fetches processing summaries for all of them.
3. It runs storedItemToLibraryItem, with its assetUrl lookups, on every item.
4. It replaces the whole items array, so every visible card re-renders.

With thousands of items this happens after every finished OCR or embedding job.

GOAL: when the backend reports that specific items changed (a job finished, a thumbnail or poster landed, etc.), update just those items in place. Fetch them with the existing getItem, or batch them if a call already exists, plus getProcessingSummaries for those ids. Keep unchanged items referentially identical so memoized cards don't re-render. Full reloads stay where they're genuinely needed: the initial load, query/view changes, imports, and anything without an item id.

STEPS:
- First find how updates reach the renderer. Look for an onItemUpdated/job lifecycle event in electron/preload.cjs, src/electron.d.ts, src/lib/libraryApi.ts, and the job queue's onUpdated/announce in electron/storage.mjs and electron/main.mjs. Find out what it carries and what currently triggers the full refresh. If the event already carries item ids, use them. If not, add the id with the smallest change.
- Coalesce bursts: a short batch of changed ids applied together is fine. Don't reintroduce per-keystroke work.

CONSTRAINTS:
- An item may have been archived, deleted or filtered out by the current query/view since. Make sure a patched item doesn't appear where it doesn't belong. When in doubt for that item, falling back to the full reload is acceptable.
- The full-refresh code re-applies session state: the note body cache and unconfirmed pins ("A refresh can resolve with data older than two writes this session already made..."). Your patch path must keep those guarantees for patched items.
- Keep the active job count (countActiveJobs) updating, since the mascot depends on it.
- Preview mode (shouldUseSeedLibrary / no desktop backend) must be unaffected.

TESTS: if you extract a pure helper (e.g. merging patched items into the list while preserving the identity of untouched ones), add a focused bun test for it. Don't add render-to-markup tests. Run:
- `bun test <files you touched>`;
- `bunx biome check <changed files>`;
- `bun run typecheck`, checking the exit code with `echo $?` and not through a pipe.

REPORT (under 200 words):
- files changed;
- which events now patch and which still fully reload;
- how the session-state guarantees are kept;
- tests run with results;
- any risk you see.

content.text:
I fixed the crash Luna hit and set the window to 1280×720, and the simpler job-status change is in. The incremental refresh is still being written.

**The crash.** OCR runs in a worker that the installed app keeps outside its main bundle (`app.asar`), but the worker's own dependencies, `regenerator-runtime` among them, were packed inside it, where the worker can't reach them. So the installed app crashed as soon as OCR started. The fix is to add those dependencies to `asarUnpack` in `package.json`. This was already wrong before the redesign, so I committed it to `feat/glass-surface` (#170) and merged that into the perf branch. 3. Failed and retried jobs show the right status.
4. The window opens at 1280×720.
5. Thumbnails finish after a restart if one was interrupted.
6. A quick regression pass over round 1.

content.text:
I fixed it, and it's pushed to #174. It wasn't serious: one full reload every 30 seconds, plus one each time you switched back to the window, even when nothing had changed. In a big library that's wasted work, though.

**What it does now:** the safety refresh and the refresh when you come back to the window still run, but they ask the database first whether anything has been written since the last full load. That uses SQLite's built-in `total_changes()` counter. Only if the number has moved does it do the full reload, so an idle library is never re-read.

**What it keeps:** the safety net for missed updates still works. Any write moves the counter, even one whose update event got lost, and the next check reloads.

**Limits:**
- While background jobs are running, the counter keeps moving, so you still get a full reload every 30 seconds then, the same as before. Once the work settles there's one final reload, and after that none until something changes.
- The counter only counts writes made by the main process. That's fine today because nothing else writes to the database.

**Checks:** a new test confirms the counter stays the same on reads and moves on writes, and typecheck and Biome are clean. It hasn't been run in the real app. Luna's round 3 is testing the build from before this change, so this part will need its own check.

Round 3 got through most of the list. The one "fail" it reported doesn't hold up, but it also means the incremental refresh still hasn't actually been tested.

**Passed**
- **OCR in the installed app:** text in a captured image was found by search ("quasar meadow"). There was no error dialog and no "Cannot find module" in the logs, so the crash fix holds.
- **Window size:** it opens at 1280×720. The 1296×728 Luna measured includes the window frame.
- **Archive tab and Settings:** both still work.

**The incremental refresh "fail" is a flaw in the test.** Luna marked a card, then captured a new image, and saw the marked card's element get replaced and the cards reorder. That's expected:
- Capturing adds the new card at the top of the grid.
- The masonry grid component identifies cards by position, not by item (`App.tsx:4154`). Adding a card at the top moves every card down one position, so every card's element gets replaced.
- That has always happened on capture and isn't from this PR.

The real check is different: leave the list alone, let a job finish on an existing item (for example, retry its OCR), and confirm the other cards' elements survive. Luna didn't run that.

**Not tested**
- Failed then retried job status.
- Recovering an interrupted thumbnail job: the jobs finished before the app quit.
- Video posters and seeking: there was no video in its test library.
- Job updates during a search, and archiving or deleting an item while its jobs run.
- The mascot settling back to idle.
- The skip-reload-when-nothing-changed change, which I made after this build.

**Harmless noise**
- Tesseract logs "Image too small to scale" for small test images.
- The `app-update.yml` error happens because `build:dir` builds don't include update metadata; it's unrelated to these changes.

If you want, I can send Luna one more short round on a fresh build covering just the gaps above. Otherwise #174 is ready for you to review.

Luna's round 4 confirmed the `app-update.yml` fix: the error no longer appears at launch. It also found two real bugs, both now fixed and pushed to #174. Their tests pass, but neither fix has been run in the app yet; round 5 is checking them now.

**Passed in round 4:**
- A job finishing during a search refreshes the results.
- Archiving and then deleting an item while its jobs run leaves no leftover card.
- The mascot and active job count settle back to idle.
- Video: the grid shows the poster without loading the video, and the detail view plays and seeks.
- The idle check is only partly confirmed. Nothing in the grid changed over 65 seconds, but Luna counted page updates rather than reload calls, and it could only simulate switching back to the window.

**Bugs found and fixed:**
1. **A card jumped to the top when OCR finished.** The library is sorted by last-updated time, and saving OCR text was bumping that time. So any full reload moved the image to the top and redrew the grid. This is older than the perf work. OCR no longer changes the last-updated time, so the grid order stays put.
2. **A corrupt image opened a native error dialog.** The bad JPEG went straight into tesseract, whose worker throws in a way that crashes into the main process. Images are now decoded first, so a corrupt one just fails its OCR job quietly. A new test covers it.

**Round 5** is checking:
- an existing item's OCR finishing leaves every other card in place;
- the corrupt image fails with no dialog;
- the failed-then-retried status on the card and in the item view, which round 4 couldn't reach because the dialog got in the way;
- OCR search, video posters and the Archive tab still work.

content.text:
I added a screenshots section to the #174 description: https://github.com/Squidys-Tools/inkling/pull/174

It has four shots from Luna's last test run in the packaged app:
- the grid, with the video card showing its poster and the cards still in place after text recognition finished
- the Archive tab
- the video playing and seeking
- a corrupt image that showed no error dialog and stayed in its spot

All four are "after" shots only. Luna never captured the app before this change, so the description says that in one line. If you want real before/after pairs, I can build the base branch and take matching shots.

The images are hosted in a secret gist, the same way #170's are. I also removed "No run in the real app yet" from the "Not done" list, since the app has now been tested.

okay some things I noticed that really gotta be fixed in the app: 

for some reason the back button does not work when entering some items details. the first item in the seeded demo library when you run the desktop app command, I clicked on it, it opened details, and when I used the back button nothing happens. this seems to work with all the other items though.

oh yeah and way too much whitespace in the sidebar in this area and the mascot is pitifully tiny [Image: image.png; ref=image_9de9e945-265a-4a0b-ab4d-266598cda4d1] 

also ive decided I dont want content in the library grid by default going all the way up to the blue line, I want it to go at max by default to the magenta/red line [Image: image.png; ref=image_74f2f8fc-a831-4cf1-b10f-d4313f38f567] 

get rid of the pointed text in settings but leave the highlighted [Image: image.png; ref=image_2b96aa6c-7280-45ed-a629-246d8cf31877]

I fixed all eight things you flagged. They're pushed to the redesign PR #170 as `e09816e`. I checked them in the Electron shell (`dev:app` with the demo library), and Biome and the typecheck pass on the changed files.

- **Back button on the first item:** this was a real bug. To close an item, the app first scrolls its card into view. The first card was partly hidden under the toolbar and the list couldn't scroll any higher, so it waited forever. It now stops when the list can't move. Back closes the first item now.
- **Item view:** it now fills the same area as the grid. It no longer covers the sidebar's collapse tab, and the gaps above and below are close to even.
- **Grid top:** the first row now starts just below the toolbar, at your magenta line. Cards still slide under the toolbar when you scroll.
- **Serendipity:** back/forward and search are gone. The "12 older saves in this walk" row was the overlapping text, and I removed it; "28 older items left" already says the same thing. The content also sits lower.
- **Empty Spaces:** the view toggle and search are hidden, and the "Nothing surfaced yet" box sits lower.
- **Sidebar:** the mascot is drawn at full size, with less space above it and below it.
- **Settings:** General is now above Library, and "Everything stays on this machine." is gone. The version line stays.

# @liquid-dom/react

## Description

`@liquid-dom/react` provides React 19 bindings for the liquid-glass layout API. It lets React describe a layout scene while the renderer mutates layout nodes directly between renders.

Use `LiquidCanvas` when the React package should create and own the WebGPU canvas. Use `LiquidScene` when another renderer, such as a Three adapter, owns the output.

## Install

```sh
pnpm add @liquid-dom/react react react-dom
```

## Quick Start

```tsx
import {
  Frame,
  Glass,
  GlassContainer,
  Html,
  LiquidCanvas,
} from '@liquid-dom/react'

export function App() {
  return (
    <LiquidCanvas style={{ width: '100vw', height: '100vh' }}>
      <GlassContainer blur={12} spacing={28}>
        <Frame width={280} height={160}>
          <Glass cornerRadius={44} pointerEvents>
            <Html sizing="fill">
              <button>Native content</button>
            </Html>
          </Glass>
        </Frame>
      </GlassContainer>
    </LiquidCanvas>
  )
}
```

## API Overview

### Roots

`LiquidCanvas` owns a liquid scene, a `Renderer`, a canvas, and a frame loop.

`LiquidCanvas` props:

| Prop | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `children` | Liquid DOM React children. |
| `ref` | Receives `LiquidCanvasRef`. |
| `className`, `style` | Applied to the host element. |
| `canvasClassName`, `canvasStyle` | Applied to the generated canvas. |
| `maxDpr` | Caps renderer DPR. Defaults to `2`. |
| `proposal` | Fixed layout proposal. If omitted, the host element is measured with `ResizeObserver`. |
| `frameloop` | `'always'` or `'demand'`. Defaults to `'always'`. |
| `onError` | Frame-loop error handler. |

`LiquidScene` is headless. It builds a liquid scene without creating a renderer or canvas. Use its ref from another renderer and call `update(proposal, delta)` before rendering.

`LiquidScene` props are `children`, `ref`, `onInvalidateFrame`, and `onInvalidateLayout`. `onInvalidateFrame` means a frame is needed without layout; `onInvalidateLayout` means layout is dirty before the next frame.

Ref handles:

| Ref | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| `LiquidCanvasRef` | `layoutScene`, `scene`, `renderer`, `canvas`, `invalidateLayout()`, `invalidateFrame()` |
| `LiquidSceneRef` | `layoutScene`, `scene`, `update(proposal, delta?)`, `invalidateLayout()`, `invalidateFrame()` |

### Layout Components

```tsx
import {
  Background,
  Frame,
  HStack,
  Overlay,
  Padding,
  Spacer,
  Transform,
  VStack,
  ZStack,
} from '@liquid-dom/react'
```

These components mirror the layout classes from `@liquid-dom/core/layout`.

| Component | Props |
| --- | --- |
| `HStack`, `VStack` | `children`, `ref`, `spacing`, `alignment`, `transition` |
| `ZStack` | `children`, `ref`, `alignment`, `transition` |
| `Frame` | `children`, `ref`, `width`, `height`, `minWidth`, `minHeight`, `idealWidth`, `idealHeight`, `maxWidth`, `maxHeight`, `alignment`, `transition` |
| `Padding` | `children`, `ref`, `insets`, `transition` |
| `Background` | `children`, `background`, `ref`, `alignment`, `transition` |
| `Overlay` | `children`, `overlay`, `ref`, `alignment`, `transition` |
| `Transform` | `children`, `ref`, `x`, `y`, `scaleX`, `scaleY`, `rotation`, `origin`, `transition` |
| `Spacer` | `ref`, `minLength`, `transition` |

`HStack`, `VStack`, and `ZStack` arrange children. `Frame`, `Padding`, and `Spacer` constrain or expand layout. `Background` and `Overlay` add decoration slots that do not affect content size. `Transform` applies scene transforms after layout. Its `origin` is a unit point in the measured layout bounds, where `{ x: 0, y: 0 }` is top-left and `{ x: 0.5, y: 0.5 }` is center.

All layout components expose refs to their nodes and accept a `transition` prop for animatable property changes.

Some layout components accept exactly one direct child: `Frame`, `Padding`, `Transform`, `GlassContainer`, and `Glass`. If you need multiple children inside one of these components, wrap them in a multi-child layout component such as `HStack`, `VStack`, or `ZStack`, then pass that wrapper as the single child.

### Glass Components

```tsx
import { Glass, GlassContainer, Html } from '@liquid-dom/react'
```

- `GlassContainer` owns the optical settings shared by its glass children, including blur, spacing, tint, refraction, specular, and shadow options.
- `Glass` defines one smooth rounded-rectangle glass shape and can opt into pointer events.
- `Html` renders React children into a DOM element owned by the `Html` node.

`GlassContainer` props:

| Group | Props |
| --- | --- |
| Shape and fusion | `spacing`, `normalDivergenceBlendPower`, `normalDivergenceBlendEnabled` |
| Blur and displacement | `blur`, `bezelWidth`, `displacementFactor`, `displacementBlur`, `debugDisplacement` |
| Refraction | `thickness`, `ior`, `contentIor`, `contentDepth`, `dispersion`, `surfaceProfile` |
| Specular and reflection | `lightDirection`, `specularStrength`, `specularWidth`, `specularFalloff`, `oppositeSpecularStrength`, `specularSharpness`, `specularOpacity`, `reflectionOffset` |
| Color and shadow | `tint`, `shadowColor`, `shadowOffsetX`, `shadowOffsetY`, `shadowBlur`, `shadowSpread` |
| Compositing and React | `opacity`, `zIndex`, `children`, `ref`, `transition` |

`Glass` shape props include uniform `cornerRadius` and analytic `cornerSmoothing`:

```tsx
<Glass
  cornerRadius={32}
  cornerSmoothing={0.6}
/>
```

`cornerSmoothing={0}` produces circular rounded-rectangle corners. Higher values use a fuller p-norm corner curve; the default `0.6` is tuned for an iOS-like squircle. Very constrained corners automatically reduce smoothing back toward a circular shape.

`Glass` props are `children`, `ref`, `cornerRadius`, `cornerSmoothing`, `pointerEvents`, `zIndex`, `onHover`, `onPress`, `onClick`, `onPointerEnter`, `onPointerLeave`, `onPointerMove`, `onPointerDown`, `onPointerUp`, `onPointerCancel`, and `transition`. Pointer handlers receive `GlassPointerEvent`; `onHover` and `onPress` receive booleans.

`Html` supports `sizing="intrinsic"`, `sizing="constrained-width"`, and `sizing="fill"`.

`Html` also supports renderer-backed compositing props:

- `opacity`: final opacity used when compositing the DOM-backed content.
- `blur`: GPU blur radius in CSS pixels. This does not use CSS filters; the renderer blurs the copied HTML texture before compositing it.
- `zIndex`: scene draw order among sibling scene or glass HTML nodes.

These props are animatable:

```tsx
<Html
  blur={open ? 0 : 12}
  opacity={open ? 1 : 0}
  sizing="fill"
  transition={{
    blur: easing({ duration: 0.25, ease: Easing.easeOut }),
    opacity: spring({ stiffness: 300, damping: 30 }),
  }}
>
  <MenuContent />
</Html>
```

`Html` props are `children`, `ref`, `sizing`, `opacity`, `blur`, `zIndex`, and `transition`.

### Node Relationship Rules

React components ultimately synchronize into the `@liquid-dom/core` scene graph, so nested children must satisfy the underlying parent rules:

- `GlassContainer` is the parent for `Glass` shapes.
- `Glass` is the parent for `Html` content.
- `Glass` cannot be nested under another `Glass`.
- Layout components do not make an invalid scene relationship valid.

For example, a `Glass` nested under `Frame` or `Transform` inside another `Glass` is still invalid, because all nested children are checked against the nearest glass scene parent.

### Hover And Press

`onHover` and `onPress` receive the same interaction state as booleans. They are useful when the interaction should drive a parent or sibling component:

```tsx
const [pressed, setPressed] = useState(false)

<Transform
  scaleX={pressed ? 0.96 : 1}
  scaleY={pressed ? 0.96 : 1}
  transition={{ scaleX: spring(), scaleY: spring() }}
>
  <Glass onPress={setPressed} />
</Transform>
```

### Animation

```tsx
import {
  AnimationConfigProvider,
  Easing,
  easing,
  spring,
  useAnimate,
  useFrame,
  useInvalidateFrame,
  useInvalidateLayout,
  useLiquidScene,
  useRenderer,
  useTimeline,
} from '@liquid-dom/react'
```

Declarative prop animation uses `transition`:

```tsx
<Frame
  width={expanded ? 260 : 140}
  height={120}
  transition={{
    width: spring({ stiffness: 360, damping: 34 }),
  }}
/>
```

Only properties listed in `transition` animate. Numeric values and numeric object values can animate; strings, booleans, and enums snap.

`spring()` creates physics-based transitions. `easing()` creates duration-based transitions:

```tsx
<Frame
  width={expanded ? 260 : 140}
  transition={{
    width: easing({
      duration: 0.25,
      ease: Easing.bezier(0.8, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8),
    }),
  }}
/>
```

Easing durations are in seconds. `ease` receives normalized progress from `0` to `1` and returns normalized progress. The convenience `Easing` namespace provides `linear`, `easeIn`, `easeOut`, `easeInOut`, and CSS-style `bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)`.

When an active easing animation is retargeted, it starts a new easing transition from the current interpolated value to the new target. `duration <= 0` snaps immediately.

`AnimationConfigProvider` scales animation time for components and hooks below it:

```tsx
<AnimationConfigProvider timeScale={0.5}>
  <Frame
    width={expanded ? 260 : 140}
    transition={{ width: spring() }}
  />
</AnimationConfigProvider>
```

`timeScale={2}` runs animations twice as fast, and `timeScale={0.5}` runs them at half speed. It applies to declarative `transition` props, `useAnimate()`, and `useTimeline()` calls under the provider. Active animations respond when `timeScale` changes. Invalid or nonpositive values are treated as `1`.

`AnimationConfigProviderProps` is `{ children?: ReactNode; timeScale?: number }`.

Animation and frame APIs:

| API | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `spring(options?)` | Creates a spring transition. Options are `stiffness`, `damping`, `mass`, `velocity`, `restSpeed`, and `restDelta`. |
| `easing(options?)` | Creates a duration transition. Options are `duration` in seconds and `ease`. |
| `Easing` | Provides `linear`, `easeIn`, `easeOut`, `easeInOut`, and `bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)`. |
| `transition` prop | Accepts a single `AnimationConfig` or a per-property `TransitionMap` with optional `default`. |
| `useAnimate()` | Starts direct node animations and returns `AnimationControls` with `finished` and `stop()`. |
| `useTimeline(defaultTransition?)` | Creates an `AnimationTimeline` with `to(target, values, transition?)`, `call(callback)`, `play()`, and `stop()`. |
| `useFrame(callback, priority?)` | Registers a callback in the nearest `LiquidCanvas` frame loop. |
| `useInvalidateLayout()` | Returns the nearest root's layout invalidation function. |
| `useInvalidateFrame()` | Returns the nearest root's frame invalidation function. |
| `useLiquidScene()` | Returns the nearest `LayoutScene`. |
| `useRenderer()` | Returns the nearest `Renderer`; only valid under `LiquidCanvas`. |

`FrameState` passed to `useFrame` includes `layoutScene`, `renderer`, `scene`, `canvas`, `time`, `delta`, `invalidateLayout`, and `invalidateFrame`.

Low-level exports include `AnimationManager`, `AnimationTimeline`, `AnimationConfig`, `ComponentTransition`, `TransitionMap`, `SpringTransition`, `EasingTransition`, `EasingFunction`, `AnimationControls`, `AnimateFunction`, and `AnimationTimeScaleRef`.

### Exported Types

Props and refs are exported for all components: `LiquidCanvasProps`, `LiquidCanvasRef`, `LiquidSceneProps`, `LiquidSceneRef`, `HStackProps`, `HStackRef`, `VStackProps`, `VStackRef`, `ZStackProps`, `ZStackRef`, `FrameProps`, `FrameRef`, `PaddingProps`, `PaddingRef`, `BackgroundProps`, `BackgroundRef`, `OverlayProps`, `OverlayRef`, `TransformProps`, `TransformRef`, `GlassContainerProps`, `GlassContainerRef`, `GlassProps`, `GlassRef`, `HtmlProps`, `HtmlRef`, `SpacerProps`, and `SpacerRef`.

Interaction handler types are `GlassPointerHandler` and `GlassStateHandler`. Root and frame-loop types are `FrameCallback` and `FrameLoopMode`.

## Integration Notes

- React 19 is required.
- Rendering requires WebGPU through `@liquid-dom/core`.
- DOM-backed `Html` content requires the experimental HTML-in-Canvas API, currently available only behind Chrome's Canvas Draw Element flag: `chrome://flags/#canvas-draw-element`.
- `LiquidCanvas` is the only root that exposes `useRenderer()`. Calling `useRenderer()` under `LiquidScene` throws.
- `LiquidScene` exposes `onInvalidateFrame` and `onInvalidateLayout` so external renderers can support demand-driven rendering.
- React children inside `Html` are portaled into layout-owned DOM hosts.
- The layout scene mutates outside React render. Use refs and hooks for imperative animation and renderer interop.
- Reference: [WICG HTML-in-Canvas](https://wicg.github.io/html-in-canvas/).

## Local Development

```sh
pnpm --filter @liquid-dom/react build
pnpm --filter @liquid-dom/react test
pnpm --filter @liquid-dom/react watch
```
